header:
Hot economy, split Fed
What it means for you

lines.text: Two Fed officials voted to raise your interest rates.
lines.say: Two Fed officials voted to raise your interest rates.

lines.text: They lost, 10-2. But the economy is running hot, prices aren't cooling, and that split reaches your wallet.
lines.say: They lost, ten to two. But the economy is running hot, prices aren't cooling off, and that split reaches straight into your wallet.

lines.text: Oct 28: the Fed kept its key rate at 3.75%-4.00%.
lines.say: On October twenty-eighth, the Fed kept its key rate at three point seven five to four percent.

lines.text: The next morning: the economy grew at a 3.4% annual pace in Q3.
lines.say: The very next morning, the government said the economy grew at a three point four percent annual pace from July through September.

lines.text: Same morning: the Fed's favorite inflation gauge was up 3.6% from a year earlier.
lines.say: That same morning, the Fed's favorite inflation gauge showed prices up three point six percent from a year earlier.

lines.text: Put it together: a hot economy, sticky prices, and a Fed that can't agree.
lines.say: Put it together and you get a strange mix: a hot economy, sticky prices, and a Fed that can't agree.

lines.text: That mix touches your card, your savings, your mortgage, your job and your 401(k).
lines.say: And that mix touches your credit card, your savings, your mortgage, your job, and your four oh one K.

lines.text: Coming up: what happened, why it's hot, why the Fed split, and your money.
lines.say: Here's the plan: what happened, why the economy is so hot, why the Fed split, and what it all means for your money.

lines.text: Chapter 1: A week of big numbers
lines.say: Let's start with the numbers, one at a time.

lines.text: First, the Fed. Rewind to December 2025: its third rate cut that year, to 3.50%-3.75%.
lines.say: First, the Fed. Rewind to December twenty twenty-five, when it made its third rate cut of that year, to three and a half to three point seven five percent.

lines.text: Sept 16, 2026: it reversed course with a quarter-point hike, its first since July 2023.
lines.say: Then on September sixteenth, twenty twenty-six, it reversed course with a quarter-point hike, its first since July twenty twenty-three.

lines.text: Oct 28: a hold. But not a unanimous one.
lines.say: And on October twenty-eighth, it held. But not unanimously.

lines.text: Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wanted another quarter-point hike.
lines.say: Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack voted no. Both wanted another quarter-point hike.

lines.text: NBC News reported it was Cook's first dissent since joining the Fed's board in 2022.
lines.say: NBC News reported it was Cook's first dissent since she joined the Fed's board in twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: The Fed's statement: "Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace."
lines.say: And the Fed's own statement opened its read on the economy with this: Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace.

scene.text: Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace.

lines.text: Next, growth. The economy grew at a 2.5% pace in Q1 2026 and 2.2% in Q2.
lines.say: The growth numbers back that up. The economy grew at a two point five percent pace in the first quarter of twenty twenty-six, and two point two percent in the second.

lines.text: Then 3.4% in Q3, above the 3.1% economists expected, per CNBC.
lines.say: Then three point four percent in the third quarter, above the three point one percent economists expected, according to CNBC.

lines.text: Annualized = the 3-month pace, as a yearly rate. This is the first of 3 estimates.
lines.say: Quick note: annualized means the three-month pace, expressed as a yearly rate. And this is the first of three estimates.

lines.text: Shoppers led: consumer spending grew at a 3.8% pace, same as Q2.
lines.say: Shoppers led the way. Consumer spending grew at a three point eight percent pace, the same as the quarter before.

lines.text: Then prices. Sept PCE inflation: 3.6% from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August.
lines.say: Then came prices. The P C E price index was up three point six percent from a year earlier in September, up from three point four in August.

lines.text: Core PCE, without food and energy: 3.1%. Both are above the Fed's 2% goal.
lines.say: Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, was three point one percent. Both numbers sit well above the Fed's two percent goal.

lines.text: A big driver: gasoline and other energy goods jumped 9.2% in September alone.
lines.say: A big driver was energy. Gasoline and other energy goods jumped nine point two percent in September alone, CNBC reported.

lines.text: Moody's Mark Zandi estimated the war has cost the average US household about $2,000 so far, mostly via energy.
lines.say: Moody's economist Mark Zandi estimated in mid-October that the war with Iran has cost the average US household about two thousand dollars so far, mostly through higher energy costs.

lines.text: Layoffs stayed rare: jobless claims were 194,000 in the week ended Oct 24.
lines.say: Meanwhile, layoffs stayed rare. Initial jobless claims were one hundred ninety-four thousand in the week ended October twenty-fourth.

lines.text: CNBC: that's near levels last seen in the late 1960s.
lines.say: CNBC noted that's near levels last seen in the late nineteen-sixties.

lines.text: And moods improved: consumer confidence rose 7.5 points in October, to 91.7.
lines.say: Even moods improved. The Conference Board's consumer confidence index jumped seven and a half points in October, to ninety-one point seven.

lines.text: That's strong growth, few layoffs, and inflation that isn't coming down. So why so hot?
lines.say: That's strong growth, few layoffs, and inflation that isn't coming down. So why is the economy this hot?

lines.text: Chapter 2: Why it's running hot
lines.say: So what's actually powering all this?

lines.text: One answer is AI. Business spending on equipment jumped at a 20.9% annual pace in Q3.
lines.say: A big part of the answer is AI. Business spending on equipment jumped at a twenty point nine percent annual pace in the third quarter, as companies poured money into the AI build-out.

lines.text: The Fed agrees: "Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust."
lines.say: Even the Fed's statement noted it: Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust.

scene.text: Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust.

lines.text: Big Tech's results show it. Alphabet: Google Cloud revenue up 103% from a year earlier.
lines.say: You can see it in Big Tech's results. Alphabet said Google Cloud revenue more than doubled, up a hundred and three percent from a year earlier.

lines.text: Microsoft: Azure and other cloud services grew 48%.
lines.say: Microsoft said Azure and its other cloud services grew forty-eight percent.

lines.text: Amazon: AWS sales rose 39%, to $46.0B.
lines.say: And Amazon said its A W S cloud sales rose thirty-nine percent, to forty-six billion dollars.

lines.text: Our math: AWS made about 63% of Amazon's operating profit in Q3.
lines.say: By our math, A W S made about sixty-three percent of Amazon's operating profit in the quarter.

lines.text: One company's AI spending is another company's sales, and someone's paycheck.
lines.say: And one company's AI spending is another company's sales, and somebody else's paycheck.

lines.text: Rising stock prices help too, at least for some people. Here's how Mark Zandi described it to CNBC.
lines.say: Rising stock prices help too, at least for some people. Here's how Mark Zandi described it to CNBC.

lines.text: "High-net-worth consumers are enjoying the runup in AI stocks and the value of their equity holdings, and are spending with some gusto."
lines.say: High-net-worth consumers are enjoying the runup in AI stocks and the value of their equity holdings, and are spending with some gusto.

scene.text: High-net-worth consumers are enjoying the runup in AI stocks and the value of their equity holdings, and are spending with some gusto.
scene.source: Mark Zandi, Moody's, to CNBC, Oct 2026

lines.text: "Lower- and middle-income consumers are increasingly struggling with falling real wages and high rates, and are much more cautious and careful spenders."
lines.say: But, he added: Lower- and middle-income consumers are increasingly struggling with falling real wages and high rates, and are much more cautious and careful spenders.

scene.text: Lower- and middle-income consumers are increasingly struggling with falling real wages and high rates, and are much more cautious and careful spenders.
scene.source: Mark Zandi, Moody's, to CNBC, Oct 2026

lines.text: Labor Dept: after inflation, average hourly pay fell 0.7% from Sept 2025 to Sept 2026.
lines.say: The Labor Department's numbers fit that picture. After inflation, average hourly pay was down zero point seven percent from September twenty twenty-five to September twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: The growth is real. For millions of people, so is the squeeze.
lines.say: So the growth is real. And for millions of people, so is the squeeze.

lines.text: Chapter 3: Why the Fed split
lines.say: Which brings us back to the Fed, and why twelve voters looking at the same numbers landed in different places.

lines.text: The tool: raise rates, borrowing costs more, spending cools, prices can ease. The risk: jobs.
lines.say: The Fed's main tool is simple. Raise rates, and borrowing costs more, spending cools, and prices can ease. The catch is that it can also cost jobs.

lines.text: 10 voted to wait for more data. 2 wanted a quarter-point hike now.
lines.say: Ten voters chose to wait for more information. Two wanted a quarter-point hike right away.

lines.text: The statement: "The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate..."
lines.say: In the statement's words: The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's two percent goal.

scene.text: The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal.

lines.text: Chair Kevin Warsh: "We will deliver price stability. No ifs, ands, or buts."
lines.say: And Chair Kevin Warsh, at his press conference, said: We will deliver price stability. No ifs, ands, or buts.

scene.text: We will deliver price stability. No ifs, ands, or buts.

lines.text: He also said: "If you think that we're tolerating some inflation target somewhere in the twos, let us disabuse you of it."
lines.say: He also said: If you think that we're tolerating some inflation target somewhere in the twos, let us disabuse you of it.

scene.text: If you think that we're tolerating some inflation target somewhere in the twos, let us disabuse you of it.

lines.text: Translation: 2% means 2%.
lines.say: Translation: the goal is two percent. Not two point something.

lines.text: Why some want more: the top of the Fed's range is 4.00%. PCE inflation is 3.6%.
lines.say: Here's one way to see why some officials want more. The top of the Fed's range is four percent. Inflation, by the P C E measure, is three point six.

lines.text: Our math: the after-inflation, or 'real', rate is only about 0.4 point.
lines.say: Subtract one from the other, and by our math the after-inflation rate, what economists call the real rate, is only about zero point four points.

lines.text: Warsh: "While overall financial conditions are tighter, I'm unwilling and unable to call them tight."
lines.say: Warsh himself said: While overall financial conditions are tighter, I'm unwilling and unable to call them tight.

scene.text: While overall financial conditions are tighter, I'm unwilling and unable to call them tight.

lines.text: For context: the top of the Fed's range at each year-end since 2019.
lines.say: For context, here's the top of the Fed's range at the end of each year since twenty nineteen.

lines.text: Near zero in 2020 and 2021. Then 4.50% in 2022 and 5.50% in 2023, as the Fed fought the last inflation surge.
lines.say: Near zero in twenty twenty and twenty twenty-one. Then four and a half percent in twenty twenty-two, and five and a half in twenty twenty-three, as the Fed fought the last inflation surge.

lines.text: Cuts brought it to 3.75% by the end of 2025. The Sept 2026 hike took it back to 4.00%.
lines.say: Cuts brought it down to three point seven five by the end of twenty twenty-five, and September's hike took it back up to four.

lines.text: Warsh was blunt about the record: "...we wouldn't be suffering from nearly six years of inflation above target."
lines.say: Warsh was blunt about the record, too. In his words: we wouldn't be suffering from nearly six years of inflation above target.

scene.text: ...we wouldn't be suffering from nearly six years of inflation above target.

lines.text: The dilemma: move too slowly and inflation digs in. Move too fast and jobs can take the hit.
lines.say: That's the Fed's dilemma. Move too slowly, and inflation can dig in. Move too fast, and jobs can take the hit.

lines.text: Chapter 4: What it means for you
lines.say: Okay. What does all of this mean for your money?

lines.text: Credit cards: most have variable rates tied to the prime rate.
lines.say: Start with credit cards. Most have variable rates tied to the prime rate.

lines.text: Prime is usually the top of the Fed's range + 3 points. Now 7.00%.
lines.say: Prime is usually the top of the Fed's range plus three points. That's seven percent right now.

lines.text: Bankrate's average card rate: 19.67% in mid-October.
lines.say: Bankrate's national average card rate was nineteen point six seven percent in mid-October.

lines.text: LendingTree: "Credit card rates have risen for three straight months and are now at their highest levels since December 2025."
lines.say: And LendingTree's Matt Schulz told CNBC: Credit card rates have risen for three straight months and are now at their highest levels since December twenty twenty-five.

scene.text: Credit card rates have risen for three straight months and are now at their highest levels since December 2025.

lines.text: Example: on a $5,000 balance, each quarter-point move is about $12.50 a year.
lines.say: Here's the math on a hypothetical five thousand dollar balance. Every quarter-point move in the rate is about twelve dollars and fifty cents a year in interest.

lines.text: At 19.67%, that balance costs about $984 a year if it never shrinks.
lines.say: But at nineteen point six seven percent, that same balance costs about nine hundred eighty-four dollars a year if it never shrinks.

lines.text: The rate level matters far more than any single move.
lines.say: So the rate level matters far more than any single quarter-point move.

lines.text: Savings is the flip side. Citing Bankrate, CNBC says some top online savings accounts pay more than 4%.
lines.say: Savings is the flip side. Citing Bankrate, CNBC says some top online savings accounts pay more than four percent.

lines.text: Example: $10,000 at 4% earns $400 in a year. 3.6% inflation takes about $360 of buying power.
lines.say: In a simple example, ten thousand dollars at four percent earns four hundred dollars in a year, while three point six percent inflation takes about three hundred sixty dollars of buying power.

lines.text: You end up about $40 ahead, before taxes. Thin, but ahead.
lines.say: So you end up about forty dollars ahead, before taxes. Thin, but ahead.

lines.text: Mortgages follow a different path: long-term Treasury yields, more than the Fed's rate.
lines.say: Mortgages follow a different path. They track long-term Treasury yields more than the Fed's rate.

lines.text: Freddie Mac's 30-year average: 7.24% on Oct 29, down from 7.32% a week earlier.
lines.say: Freddie Mac's average thirty-year rate was seven point two four percent on October twenty-ninth, down from seven point three two a week earlier.

lines.text: A year earlier, it was 6.17%.
lines.say: A year earlier, it was six point one seven percent.

lines.text: Example: a $300,000, 30-year loan: about $1,832 a month at 6.17% vs about $2,044 at 7.24% (principal + interest).
lines.say: On a hypothetical three hundred thousand dollar, thirty-year loan, principal and interest go from about one thousand eight hundred thirty-two dollars a month at the old rate to about two thousand forty-four at the new one.

lines.text: That's about $213 more, every month.
lines.say: That's roughly two hundred thirteen dollars more, every single month, for the same loan.

lines.text: Car loans: Edmunds says "The headline new-car APR has essentially flatlined at the 7% threshold all year."
lines.say: Car loans have barely budged. Edmunds analyst Joseph Yoon told CNBC: The headline new-car A P R has essentially flatlined at the seven percent threshold all year.

scene.text: The headline new-car APR has essentially flatlined at the 7% threshold all year.

lines.text: Jobs: employers added just 29,000 jobs in September. Unemployment: 4.2%.
lines.say: Now jobs. The latest jobs report showed employers added just twenty-nine thousand jobs in September, with unemployment at four point two percent.

lines.text: Few layoffs, slow hiring: good if you have a job, a grind if you're looking.
lines.say: So layoffs are rare, but hiring is slow. That's decent news if you have a job, and a grind if you're looking for one.

lines.text: Your 401(k): when rates rise, prices of existing bonds fall, and higher rates can weigh on stocks too.
lines.say: And your four oh one K? When interest rates rise, prices of existing bonds fall, and higher rates can weigh on stock prices too.

lines.text: In 2022, as the Fed hiked fast, the S&P 500 fell 19.4%. History, not a forecast.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-two, as the Fed hiked fast, the S and P five hundred fell nineteen point four percent. That's history, not a forecast.

lines.text: Chapter 5: What to watch next
lines.say: So what comes next? Here's the calendar, and what markets are saying.

lines.text: Friday, Nov 6: the October jobs report.
lines.say: Friday, November sixth: the October jobs report.

lines.text: Tuesday, Nov 10: October consumer prices.
lines.say: Tuesday, November tenth: October consumer prices.

lines.text: Dec 8-9: the Fed's next meeting, with a decision on Dec 9 and new projections.
lines.say: And December eighth and ninth: the Fed's next meeting, with the decision on the ninth, plus new economic projections.

lines.text: Markets: on Oct 27, CME FedWatch put the odds of a December hike at about 78%, CNN reported.
lines.say: As for markets, CNN reported that on October twenty-seventh, CME's FedWatch tool put the odds of a December quarter-point hike at about seventy-eight percent.

lines.text: Right after the Oct 28 decision: about 85%.
lines.say: Right after the October twenty-eighth decision, those odds rose to about eighty-five percent.

lines.text: Odds move every day, and they aren't a decision.
lines.say: But those odds move every day, and they aren't a decision.

lines.text: Warsh: "If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today."
lines.say: Warsh put it this way: If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today.

scene.text: If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today.

lines.text: Worth watching until then: gas prices, core inflation, hiring, and your own card's rate.
lines.say: Until then, the numbers worth watching are gas prices, core inflation, hiring, and the rate on your own card statement.

lines.text: Chapter 6: The recap
lines.say: Let's wrap it up.

lines.text: The economy grew at a 3.4% pace in Q3, led by shoppers and AI spending.
lines.say: The economy grew at a three point four percent pace in the third quarter, led by shoppers and AI spending.

lines.text: Prices were up 3.6% from a year earlier in September, well above the 2% goal.
lines.say: Prices were up three point six percent from a year earlier in September, well above the Fed's two percent goal.

lines.text: The Fed held at 3.75%-4.00%, but two officials wanted a hike.
lines.say: The Fed held at three point seven five to four percent, but two officials wanted a hike.

lines.text: Card rates, savings yields and mortgages all hang on the data before Dec 9.
lines.say: So your card rate, your savings yield and your mortgage rate all hang on what the data shows before December ninth.

lines.text: A hot economy can be good news for some, and a squeeze for others, depending on which side you're on.
lines.say: A hot economy can be good news for some people, and a real squeeze for others, depending on which side of it you're on.

lines.text: That's the Big Story. See you next week.
lines.say: That's the big story of the week. Subscribe, and I'll see you next Friday.

post.title: Two Fed officials wanted a rate hike. Hot economy, 3.6% inflation: what it means for you
post.ig: The economy grew 3.4%, prices are up 3.6%, and two Fed officials voted for a hike. Here's what that split means for your card, savings and mortgage.
post.tiktok: Two Fed officials voted to raise rates. Here's why, and what it means for your money.
post.yt_desc:
The Fed held rates at 3.75%-4.00% on October 28, 2026, but two officials, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, voted for a hike. A day later, the economy posted 3.4% growth for the third quarter while the Fed's preferred inflation gauge showed prices up 3.6% from a year earlier. This video explains what happened, why the economy is running hot (shoppers and the AI build-out), why the Fed is split, and what it all means for credit cards, savings, mortgages, jobs and your 401(k), plus the dates to watch before the Dec 8-9 Fed meeting.
